prompt: Top-down still life, vertical 9:16, camera at 90 degrees over an Indian miniature painting lying flat. Full-bleed 9:16 picture edge to edge: the painted paper fills the whole frame, with no painted border, margin, ruled frame, mount, table edge, bands or panels anywhere. Reference 1 is the authority on this exact piece: copy its construction exactly and ignore its background and light. Reference 2 is a detail of the same piece. It is the clasp close up and the authority on the sailor ring's spring gate, push-pin nub, ribbed collar and the straight one-row stone bar; take nothing else from it: no skin, neck or body. THE PIECE: A 50 cm chain, 4 mm wide, of elongated paperclip links (about 4 x 11 mm) in polished 18k gold tone. 1 thick round spring-gate sailor ring about 22 mm across (about 14 mm opening, small push-pin nub, ribbed gate collar) and 1 short straight bar about 15 mm long set with 1 row of about 9 tiny clear stones, on a jump ring. No pendant, no other stones. Must stay a sailor ring with a straight bar 0.6-0.7x the ring, never a plain donut ring, a lobster clasp, or a curved or multi-row pave bar. The bar is short and slim: end to end it is 0.6 of the sailor ring's outside diameter (about 13 mm against the 22 mm ring), never longer than 0.7 of it; it is about half as thick as the ring's tube; its 9 tiny clear stones fill it from tip to tip in one row, with no plain, textured, engraved or stippled block at either end; its one jump ring is at its outer tip. Seen from above, the bar lies across the ring's upper-left tube and its inner tip stops just short of the ring's centre. On the ring, the spring gate is a thinner tube across the top, running from the main tube's flat cut end at 11 o'clock to a short barrel collar at 1 o'clock; the chain's one plain round jump ring hangs on that barrel collar, with no other fittings; the push-pin nub is a small ball on a short stem at 3 o'clock, no wider than a third of the tube; two fine ribbed grooves circle the tube at 4 o'clock, just below the nub. Last time this went wrong, so correct it: the bar grew to 0.87 of the ring, too thick, with oversized stones and an invented stone-less end block; the gate was drawn at full tube thickness and the nub was oversized and fused into a wide ribbed band; the ring sat too low and too far right; the painted gate stood more than twice the ring's height; and the dunes under the chain were brighter than the metal. Every link, the sailor ring, the bar and both jump rings are the same polished 18k gold tone, never silver tone, white metal or rose. Exactly two chain ends in the picture: the long strand that forms the road ends at the ring's barrel collar on one jump ring; a second short strand ends at the bar's one jump ring and runs off the right edge just above the gate; no third strand, no loose jump ring, no extra chain end. LAID AS A ROAD: the chain enters at the left edge and winds in one gentle S across the middle to the right, where the sailor ring lies flat, gate collar and nub visible, the bar across it; the ring is about 19% of the frame width, its centre 41% of the way down the frame and 62% across, and its right edge, nub included, at least 14% of the frame width from the right edge, every link separate. SCALE: the frame shows about 100 mm of the painting across; the ring is 22 mm, a little bigger than a one-rupee coin, each link 4 x 11 mm; the ring rests on and overlaps the 18 mm painted gate, so the door-knocker is bigger than the door, by the old painters' rule, never bigger than about a quarter of the frame. THE PAINTING (Marwar school desert at dusk, opaque gouache on burnished wasli paper, flat colour fields, fine brushwork, visible paper fibre, perfectly flat; about 10 cm in frame; an original composition in that school's manner, never a copy of any known or museum painting): ochre and saffron dunes, a calm lilac-plum dusk sky with a few small round painted fireworks in white dots, and around the ring a small white palace gate, finials included no taller than one and a half times the ring's diameter, its plum doorway narrower than the ring, its base no lower than 48% down and its top no higher than 30% down, so the ring is the biggest thing on the gate, with a scalloped arch and closed plum doors; the ring rests on the doors exactly where a door-knocker would hang. The dunes the chain crosses are a deep dusky ochre-terracotta in soft shadow, darker than the metal, so every link's bright kicker edge is the lightest, most saturated thing on the page; the paler saffron dunes stay behind the procession. On the far (upper) side of the road only, with a clear 5 mm gap of plain dune between it and the chain, walks a riderless wedding procession painted small, every animal facing and walking toward the gate: three elephants in saffron and oxblood cloths carrying kettle-drums, drumsticks raised with nobody holding them, two plumed horses with empty saddles, lamps on poles; flat profile silhouettes in gouache with no painted eye dots; each animal shorter than two links, flat brushwork on the paper, never touching, crossing or overlapping any link. No riders, mahouts, drummers or people of any kind on or beside the animals, no water. CONTACT: a fine real shadow under every link, the bar and the ring, with a thin dark contact line wherever the metal touches the paper. LIGHT, two lights only: one large soft overhead daylight, no glare; one small hard specular kicker low from the left puts a bright edge on every link and the ring, and a white catchlight in each tiny stone. COMPOSITION: piece and shadow centred in the band from 26% to 53% of the frame height; 13-25% calm and plain for a headline; below 54% calm plain ground for type. The whole chain lies between 33% and 47% of the frame height; nothing of the piece is lower than 47% down. No text, no letters, no numbers, no logos, no watermark: no script, signatures, seals, stamps or inscription panels anywhere in the painting. No painted people or deities, no faces, no eyes, no eyebrows; animals only as tiny flat profile silhouettes. One product only: no other jewellery, no props.

prompt: Top-down still life, vertical 9:16, camera at 90 degrees over an Indian miniature painting lying flat. Full-bleed 9:16 picture edge to edge: the painted paper fills the whole frame, with no painted border, margin, ruled frame, mount, table edge, bands or panels anywhere. Reference 1 is the authority on this exact piece: copy its construction exactly and ignore its background and light. Reference 2 is a detail of the same piece. It shows both studs of the pair from above and is the authority on how the two mirror each other; ignore its cube, background and light. THE PIECE (one pair): Each 16.8mm stud, 18k gold tone: 1 tilted cushion-cut deep green cubic zirconia (10mm) in a polished collet sits at 12 o'clock over a hollow circlet about 14mm wide. Clockwise round the circlet: 1 clear cubic zirconia, 1 large white shell pearl at 3 o'clock, 2 clear stones, 1 plain four-point star, 1 small pearl, 1 clear stone, 1 star centred with a clear stone. The pair mirror each other. The circlet must stay hollow and lopsided under the stone (big pearl one side, small pearl and stars the other), never a symmetric halo with the green stone in its centre. Metal: 18k gold tone, high polish. The two stars on each circlet are solid, bevelled, mirror-polished four-point stars with long, sharp, straight points, made in one piece with the circlet exactly as in reference 1; never wire outlines, open petals, leaves, butterflies, flowers or filigree. Every star point on both studs is short, the same length as that star's other points, and ends in one sharp tip on the star itself, exactly as in reference 1; no point is lengthened, doubled, kinked or joined to anything, and no part of either stud reaches out toward the pavilion, the hills or any painted object. Last time the upper stud's star centred with a clear stone grew a second faceted gold segment on its lower-left point, almost twice as long as its other points, that reached out and fused with a gilt pavilion roof; that spike does not exist on the real piece and must not appear. The circlet is a smooth, round, mirror-polished band with clean claw settings; no granulated, crinkled or textured metal. Posts, collets, claws and stars are all the same 18k gold tone. ARRANGEMENT: a straight painted horizon crosses the frame at 39.5% of its height. One stud lies face up in the sky just above it, green stone at the top, large pearl on the right. Its mirrored twin lies face up in the lake directly below, turned 180 degrees in the plane: green stone at the bottom, its large pearl also on the right under the first one's, so it mirrors the first across the horizon like a reflection. The lower stud is the exact mirror image of the upper one across the horizon line, part for part: the same size, its green stone the same size with the same tilt mirrored, every clear stone, pearl, star and claw exactly as far below the line as its partner is above it and at the same distance from the left edge. Last time the lower green stone sat a little off its mirrored partner. The bottom of the upper stud's circlet and the top of the lower stud's circlet both just touch the painted horizon line, one from above and one from below, exactly one above the other. Posts pass through pinholes in the paper so both lie flat. Each stud is small in the frame: about 19% of the frame width wide and about 12% of the frame height tall, with more than 40% of the frame width of plain painted ground on each side of it. The upper stud's green stone starts at 27% of the frame height, the horizon is at 39.5%, and the lower stud's green stone ends at 52%; nothing of either stud is above 27% or below 52% of the frame height. Last time each stud filled a third of the frame width, the horizon fell at 47% and the lower stud reached 67% of the frame height; keep both studs this small and this high. THE PAINTING (Kishangarh school night lake, opaque gouache on burnished wasli paper, flat colour fields, fine brushwork, visible paper fibre, perfectly flat; about 7 cm in frame; an original composition in that school's manner, never a copy of any known or museum painting): a flat plum-black sky with tiny shell-white dot stars; on the far shore just left of the upper stud, a tiny flat-painted white pavilion about 12 mm wide, its domed roof matte white gouache with no gold anywhere on it, the outer tip of its roof eave just touching the tip of the upper stud's left star point; its warm lamps are small flat dots of yellow paint on the side facing the studs, never glossy gold drops, and low blue-green hills; below the horizon a still lake in flat deep indigo-teal with fine pale ripple lines. Last time the pavilion roof was painted gilt and its lamps were glossy gold drops. No moon is painted. The lake is paint, not real water: no wet reflections. Paint no reflection of the pavilion or the hills and no gloss or shimmer on the lake: the only reflection in the picture is the lower stud. The sky is plum-black, a deep purple-black, never navy or blue-black. The pavilion is plain white with no carved panels, marks or patterns that could read as writing. The paper is clean and whole to every edge, with no worn, torn or folded corners. SCALE AND CONTACT: the frame shows about 70 mm of the painting across; each stud is 16.8 mm tall, a little taller than the 12 mm pavilion is wide, and its green stone is 10 mm. Each stud casts a short soft real shadow on the paper, with a thin dark contact line where the metal touches it. LIGHT, two lights only: one soft overhead daylight kept low so plum and indigo stay deep; one small hard specular kicker from the upper left gives each green stone a facet flash, clear stones white catchlights, pearls a soft sheen. COMPOSITION: the pair and its shadows inside the band from 27% to 52% of the frame height, centred left to right; 12-26% calm plain night sky for a headline; below 53% calm plain painted lake for type. No text, no letters, no numbers, no logos, no watermark: no script, signatures, seals, stamps or inscription panels anywhere in the painting. No painted people or deities, no faces, no eyes, no eyebrows; animals only as tiny flat profile silhouettes. One product only: no other jewellery, no props.
